cells.tense: You are carrying the weight now, and it is staying workable in your hands.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: Next time someone close is struggling, sit with it a few minutes — and keep your own feet, your own view, your own evening. Not merging, not fixing. Alongside.
cells.core:
You can carry a lot without going hard about it. When something you're tending is under strain, you don't clamp down and you don't drop it — you bear what's there, which is why what's around you grows without being rushed or squeezed. That's the rare part, and it's in your hands today.

Where this can still grow is at the edge of the people you're tending. When someone close is carrying something heavy, there's a pull to take all of it onto yourself. Feel what they're carrying with them instead — and keep your own side of it. Their strain doesn't have to become yours to be honoured. For now, that's the practice: closeness that doesn't dissolve the line between you.
cells.sheetLine: You hold what's heavy, and it stays workable in your hands.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be held without going rigid around it
cells.place: the care that lets something grow at its own pace

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a version of events that has not arrived yet.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: When you're carrying more than your share for someone, adjust it once — hand a piece back, or take something you've been going without — then stop counting and carry only what's yours.
cells.core:
Your strength is working too hard ahead of schedule. Nothing has gone wrong yet and you're already steadying everything that might, carrying weight nobody put on you, standing in for people who could stand themselves. What you're doing is care. It has gone past what the moment asks for.

Fairness loosens it, and fairness is a small correction, not a verdict. Somewhere in what you're carrying there's a share that isn't yours — something you took on for someone who could hold it, or something you're doing that no one asked for. Set that piece down, and it can go back to whoever it belongs to. Or take something you've been going without. Then stop counting. The load evens out and what you carry goes back to the size of the day.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for trouble that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be held without going rigid around it
cells.place: the care that lets something grow at its own pace

cells.tense: You stood at a door holding everything, and it felt too dangerous to keep holding.
cells.act: let go of the thing you are gripping
cells.ask: Take a worry, an outcome, a grip you can't open — set it down on purpose for a day. Not forever. Just set it down and notice your hands empty.
cells.core:
Holding anything feels risky now, so it stopped. When pressure came, whatever you were carrying set itself down without asking you — and the care you have for growing things went quiet with it. You're still here. This part of you didn't leave; it just isn't being trusted right now.

Gripping harder isn't what restores it. The other direction is: putting something down on purpose, the way you'd close a book at the end of a chapter rather than dropping it. Choose a worry, an outcome you can't steer, a decision you keep carrying — set it down deliberately. Not because you failed. Because it's finished with you. Empty hands for a day, and see what they feel like when something new comes to be held.
cells.sheetLine: You stood at the door with everything, and set it down.

cells.tense: You have been carrying a load for a long while and calling it nothing in particular.
cells.act: remember what drew you and face it again
cells.ask: Think of something you've been growing — a person, a project, a habit — and put into words what first drew you to it. Then look at it plainly, as it is now.
cells.core:
There's strength in how you hold things, and you don't count it as anything. What you've been tending — people, work, a life — has kept going under pressure, and your account of it is that you were just there. You've been carrying a lot and calling it circumstance.

The pull that started it is smaller and older than the load. Before all this, something drew you toward what you're now holding — you chose it, wanted it, saw it as worth tending. That pull is still the honest name for what's happening. Go back to it. Look at what you've been growing and let yourself see it as something you chose and still choose, not just a weight that landed on you. What you're holding has your fingerprints on it.
cells.sheetLine: You carry a great deal and call it nothing in particular.
